**D-Wave — the annealing schedule that decided who won the benchmark (2013–2014)**

In 2013 McGeoch and Wang benchmarked a 439-qubit D-Wave Two and reported it finishing certain QUBO instances roughly 3,600 times faster than CPLEX. The headline travelled much further than the caveats. Dash then reformulated the same instances as a mixed-integer program and reported that CPLEX solved them to optimality in at most 94 seconds on a single core — against running times of up to 1,800 seconds in the original comparison. No hardware had changed; the classical baseline had been the wrong baseline.

The careful test came in 2014, when Rønnow, Wang and colleagues published "Defining and detecting quantum speedup" in *Science*. They ran random Ising spin-glass instances on the Chimera graph of a D-Wave Two with up to 503 working qubits of the 512-qubit Vesuvius chip, and compared it against a heavily optimised multispin-coded simulated annealer on an Intel Xeon E5-2670 and against simulated quantum annealing by path-integral Monte Carlo. Because all three are stochastic heuristics, they insisted on the honest cost measure: total time to solution is the annealing time multiplied by the repetitions R = ⌈log(1−p)/log(1−s)⌉ needed to reach the ground state with 99% confidence. All three scaled alike, and the paper found no evidence of quantum speedup when the entire data set was considered.

The mechanism underneath that result is the schedule, which is why this study belongs to this lesson and not to a quantum computing one. The DW2 had a minimum annealing time of 20 µs, which the authors note is longer than the optimal annealing time for every problem size they tested. The machine was structurally unable to cool fast enough for small instances; it over-annealed them. Once you fix a schedule and let N grow, the slope you measure is no longer a property of the algorithm. The paper demonstrates this directly: a constant, suboptimal annealing time can both hide a genuine speedup and fabricate one that is not there, because the ratio of two mis-tuned time-to-solution curves has a slope of its own.

You will meet the same trap without any quantum hardware in the room. The moment you compare your annealer against a competitor — a different metaheuristic, a solver, last quarter's implementation — the comparison is only meaningful if each side runs at its own optimised schedule at each problem size. A geometric α = 0.95 tuned at n = 100 and carried unchanged to n = 10,000 does not measure your algorithm; it measures how long ago you last tuned it. Report time to a target quality with the repetition count folded in, re-tune T₀ and α per size, and treat any speedup figure that came from a fixed schedule as unproven.

**Airbus — the evolved cabin partition that only a printer could build (2015–2016)**

The A320 bionic partition was a joint project between Airbus and Autodesk Research (through its studio The Living). The part is the dividing wall between the rear galley and the passenger cabin, which also holds the cabin attendants' jumpseat — a structural component that has to pass 16G crash testing before certification for the A320 fleet. Airbus set the target at a 50% weight reduction. The team did not draw a partition; they built a generator and a fitness function and let a search find the geometry.

The pipeline had two halves. A bottom-up growth algorithm modelled on slime mould laid down candidate networks of struts between fixed structural attachment points, producing a parameterised lattice rather than a fixed shape. A genetic algorithm then drove that parameterisation, evaluating each candidate by finite element analysis against three competing objectives: minimise mass, keep stress and displacement within limits, and avoid large unsupported holes in the panel. Generations were plotted as a cloud converging on a Pareto front, because the objectives genuinely trade against one another. Published accounts report the resulting partition as roughly 45% lighter, about 30 kg saved per unit, and Airbus has estimated that applying the approach across the cabin and the A320 backlog could avoid up to 465,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year.

The cost is the part of the story a press release omits. First, the evolved lattice is not manufacturable by milling, casting or bending; it was produced by direct metal laser sintering in Scalmalloy, an aluminium-magnesium-scandium powder Airbus developed for printing, as 122 separate printed parts run in seven batches and then assembled. The search space was implicitly the set of printable structures, and a design encoding that had not been constrained that way would have converged on beautiful geometry no supplier could deliver. Second, every fitness evaluation is an FEA run. That single fact dominates the algorithm design: population size, generation count and mutation strength are all rationed against simulation cost, not against theory. Third, the output is a front, not a winner — an engineer still chose the point on it, and then had to defend that choice through certification.

When you reach for a GA on a real engineering problem, these three constraints are the design, and the textbook knobs are secondary. Ask what your fitness evaluation costs before you choose µ and λ; ask whether your encoding can even express an infeasible artefact, because if it can, selection will find it; and decide in advance whether you want a scalarised objective or a Pareto front you are prepared to argue about with somebody who has to sign it off.

**Migros — ant colony routing that replaced the overnight planning shift (2006–2007)**

AntRoute is a commercial routing product from AntOptima, a spin-off of IDSIA, the Swiss AI institute where much of the ant colony optimisation literature originated. Its tour optimiser is an Ant Colony System, and the deployment that made it interesting is Migros, the largest Swiss supermarket chain, whose daily distribution runs on a fleet of hundreds of trucks. The published description of the product is blunt about what it is for: optimising thousands of daily orders in a few minutes while respecting the real constraints — fleet composition, customer time windows, unit loads, access limitations by vehicle type, multiple depots. In the account Rizzoli, Montemanni and Gambardella give of the deployment, the colony produced its plan in minutes against human planners who needed hours for the same day's orders, and produced better ones.

What it actually beat is worth being precise about. It was not competing with an exact solver — nobody solves a national grocery distribution instance to optimality overnight. It was competing with experienced dispatchers working from stable, historically grown routes plus manual repair. That baseline is strong on constraints the model omits and weak exactly where combinatorial search is strong: it rarely reconsiders which customers go on which vehicle, because a human will not tear up a working route sheet for a marginal saving.

The mechanism that earns ACO its place here is the pheromone matrix as memory. Demand is largely periodic — the same stores, similar volumes, week on week — so the trails learned on one day's instance are a warm start for the next, and for orders arriving after the planning cut-off the colony can be restarted from the conserved matrix rather than from a uniform τ₀. That is the reason a constructive metaheuristic beats a from-scratch improvement heuristic under a hard clock. The counterweight is stagnation: reinforcing yesterday's structure is precisely how a colony stops exploring, which is why evaporation and MAX-MIN style bounds stop being tuning details and become the safety mechanism keeping the plan responsive to a changed network.

There is an adoption cost that shows up in every deployment of this kind and rarely in the papers. A pheromone-driven plan is not explainable to the dispatcher who has to sign it; it changes shape day to day, and the drivers notice. When you deploy ACO into a planning function, budget for that: hold some structure stable deliberately, expose the constraint violations you are trading against, and decide up front whether the operator is allowed to override the colony — because they will, and your evaporation rate then determines how long that override survives in the trails.

**Netherlands Railways — the national timetable that integer programming could not build (2003–2009)**

In December 2006 Netherlands Railways introduced a timetable built from scratch to replace the 1970 one, covering about 5,500 daily trains. The requirement was contradictory: run more trains on infrastructure barely extended since the war while improving punctuality. Kroon and colleagues describe it in *Interfaces*. Cyclic timetabling became a periodic event scheduling problem — every arrival, departure, junction passage and bridge opening is an event, and running times, dwell times and headways constrain differences of event times, modulo 60 for the hourly cycle.

Small instances of that model can be solved as a MIP. The real one cannot. A typical NS instance has approximately 8,400 events and about 70,000 PESP constraints, and because each constraint introduces a binary variable encoding the order of two trains, the LP relaxation is very weak. The team built CADANS instead: a constraint programming module aimed squarely at feasibility, with special-purpose propagation and, in their words, particular attention to backtracking from infeasible branches of the tree. Computing time is often only a few minutes.

What matters most is what CADANS does when there is no solution. It returns a feasible timetable satisfying all PESP constraints if one exists; if none exists it identifies the conflicting constraints and shows how to resolve the infeasibility, so the planner can relax one — a transfer guarantee at a station, say — and rerun. Over-constraint is the normal state at this size, and a solver that answers only "infeasible" would have been useless. That turned the exercise into an iterative design conversation: ten timetable variants were produced, and the board picked two, then asked for an eleventh combining them.

The trade-off is explicit: propagation gives feasibility, not optimality — the CP techniques provide no facility for direct optimisation — so a separate post-optimisation pass shifts arrival and departure times within the fixed structure to improve transfers. NS conservatively estimated an extra annual profit of €10 million in 2007, rising to €20 million later; a record 86.8% punctuality in 2007 triggered an agreed 2% bonus fare rise worth about €20 million a year from 2008. It was not politically clean: when the plans were published in spring 2006 the reaction in parts of the country was hostile, because a national re-optimisation makes somebody's journey worse.

When you model a real scheduling problem as a CSP, design for the infeasible case first. Decide which constraints are negotiable before you write them, keep the propagator able to return a conflict set rather than a bare failure, and hold feasibility apart from optimisation.

**DIMACS — the routing challenge that memetic algorithms settled (2021–2022)**

The 12th DIMACS Implementation Challenge put vehicle routing on a common footing: fixed instances, a single run per instance, and solvers scored by primal integral — gap to a reference solution integrated over time, so a method that is slow to a good tour is penalised against one decent within seconds. The VRPTW track used the 56 Solomon and 300 Gehring & Homberger instances. What it settled is architectural: hybrid genetic search — a population method in which every offspring is handed to a local search before it may compete — was shown state of the art there.

Kool and colleagues' entry, Router, is a clean illustration because they documented it: built on the open-source HGS-CVRP implementation with time windows added, it is textbook memetic — 100 initial solutions built by SPLIT over random customer orderings, binary tournament selection, ordered crossover plus a Selective Route Exchange operator that swaps whole routes between parents, then local search on the offspring — the education phase — and survivor culling down from µ + λ (25 + 40) by a fitness that combines solution quality with diversity. It ranked first in Phase 1 of the VRPTW track and improved best-known solutions on Gehring & Homberger instances for the distance-only objective.

The mechanism carrying the load is not crossover but the deliberate cultivation of infeasibility. HGS maintains two pools, one feasible and one infeasible, with parents drawn from either. Constraint violations are priced rather than forbidden: the capacity penalty is auto-adjusted so that roughly 20% of local searches end in a feasible solution, and the time-window penalty is raised 20% when fewer than 15% of local-search results are feasible and lowered 15% when more than 25% are. The search is held on the boundary, where the good solutions of a tightly constrained routing problem live.

The trade-off in their write-up is the kind of finding that only shows up in a real run. When no feasible solution has yet been found they apply a temporary penalty booster, doubling the weight — but starting from a large penalty instead "lets the algorithm converge too quickly to suboptimal solutions, hurting final performance". The obvious fix, price violations heavily from the start, is the wrong one: it collapses diversity before local search has anything to work with.

When you build a memetic algorithm, this is where your attention belongs. The crossover and mutation rates of a plain GA matter far less than the local-search budget per offspring, the mechanism preserving diversity against an operator whose entire job is to destroy it, and the penalty schedule deciding how far outside the feasible region your population is allowed to live.
